title: Indonesia should not copy the green plans of rich countries
gist: The authors argue Indonesia should not mimic subsidy-heavy US/EU green industrial policy because of its 3%-of-GDP deficit cap, premature deindustrialisation (manufacturing down from ~32% to ~19% of GDP) and ~60% informal workforce. Instead it should pursue resource-based policy built on its nickel export ban and use the October 2026 IMF/World Bank meetings in Bangkok to seek cheap long-term finance and state-capacity support, judged by jobs and wages.

insights.claim: US and EU green industrial policies such as the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act and the 2024 EU Net-Zero Industry Act share the goal of reshoring factories, reducing dependence on China and protecting domestic jobs, with competition and security mattering as much as climate.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Western clean-tech policy is driven by security and reshoring motives, which shapes durability and trade friction with China.
insights.quote: Rich countries want to bring factories home, depend less on China and protect jobs for their own workers. Climate matters, but competition and security matter just as much.

insights.claim: The EU Net-Zero Industry Act adopted in 2024 aims for at least 40% of the clean technology Europe needs to be made inside Europe by 2030, while US Inflation Reduction Act clean-energy tax credits were cut back under the Trump administration.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Divergent US and EU clean-tech support affects where clean-tech manufacturing demand and subsidies will concentrate.
insights.quote: aims to make at least 40% of the clean technology Europe needs inside Europe by 2030

insights.claim: The World Bank has reversed its decades-long advice to leave industry to the market, accepting in its 2026 report 'Industrial Policy for Development: Approaches in the 21st Century' that governments can play an active role in building industries.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Multilateral acceptance of industrial policy lowers resistance to state-led interventions like export bans across emerging markets.
insights.quote: For decades, it advised developing countries to leave industry to the market.

insights.claim: Indonesia's law caps the budget deficit at 3% of GDP, the Finance Minister projected in August 2026 that the year's deficit would reach about 2.85%, and Parliament is debating whether to change the limit.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: A near-cap deficit and possible change to the fiscal rule is a key risk factor for Indonesian sovereign bonds and the rupiah.
insights.quote: In August, the Finance Minister projected (Opens in new window) that this year’s deficit would reach about 2.85%. Parliament is debating whether to change the limit.
insights.locator: First, Indonesia does not have the same money.

insights.claim: Manufacturing has fallen from about 32% of the Indonesian economy in the early 2000s to around 19% today, a case of premature deindustrialisation in which factories shrink before the country becomes rich.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Shrinking manufacturing share undermines Indonesia's growth model and middle-income escape prospects.
insights.quote: Economists call this “premature deindustrialisation”: factories are shrinking before the country has become rich.
insights.locator: Second, the starting point is different.

insights.claim: Around 60% of Indonesian workers earn their living in informal jobs without contracts or insurance, so Indonesia's industrial policy must focus on creating good jobs rather than protecting existing factory jobs as US policy does.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Job creation, not capital-intensive output, should be the metric for evaluating Indonesian industrial policy success.
insights.quote: Indonesia must ask how to create good jobs for millions of people who have never had one.

insights.claim: The World Bank has warned that Indonesia's goal of becoming a high-income country by 2045 will need something close to a 'miracle', as many countries get stuck at middle income for decades.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Long-run Indonesian growth expectations embedded in policy targets are likely too optimistic.
insights.quote: The World Bank has warned (Opens in new window) that this goal will need something close to a “miracle”.

insights.claim: Because Indonesia is fiscally constrained, a US-style trillion-dollar subsidy programme would divert money from schools, health and roads, so Indonesia should learn from but not copy rich-country green plans.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Expect Indonesia to lean on regulation and resource leverage rather than large subsidies for clean-tech industrialisation.
insights.quote: Either way, a trillion-dollar subsidy program would take money away from schools, health and roads.
insights.locator: First, Indonesia does not have the same money.

insights.claim: Indonesia, which holds the world's largest nickel reserves, banned raw nickel ore exports in 2020 to force domestic processing, an industrial policy based on resources rather than large subsidies.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Indonesia's export ban structurally shapes global battery-metal supply and processing location.
insights.quote: In 2020, the government banned (Opens in new window) the export of raw nickel ore to push companies to process it here.

insights.claim: In 2023 the IMF called on Indonesia to lift its ban on raw mineral exports and not extend it to other minerals, and Indonesia refused.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Indonesia is willing to defy the IMF on resource nationalism, signalling policy persistence and potential extension to other minerals.
insights.quote: In 2023, it called on (Opens in new window) Indonesia to lift its ban on raw mineral exports and not to extend it to other minerals. Indonesia refused.
insights.locator: The IMF has not always been helpful.

insights.claim: A World Bank study found an earlier version of Indonesia's mineral export ban raised the value added to exports but also drew in small, inefficient firms, which the authors read as a case for better design rather than abandoning the policy.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Export bans can lift value-added but risk inefficient capacity, relevant for assessing Indonesian processing-sector economics.
insights.quote: The lesson is better design, not dropping the policy.

insights.claim: More than 94% of the power used to process nickel in Indonesia comes from coal, and a budget near its legal limit cannot pay to clean that up.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Coal-heavy Indonesian nickel faces ESG and carbon-border risk for EV battery buyers unless concessional finance decarbonises it.
insights.quote: More than 94% of the power used to process nickel comes (Opens in new window) from coal.

insights.claim: Joining new energy-transition supply chains early could help Indonesia escape the middle-income trap, because early entrants learn new skills and build new industries.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Indonesia's push into battery supply chains is a core development strategy, implying continued policy support for downstream investment.
insights.quote: countries that join new supply chains early can learn new skills and build new industries
insights.locator: The energy transition could help Indonesia

themes.theme: Asks for the IMF/World Bank Bangkok meetings

insights.claim: World Bank chief economist Indermit Gill names three conditions for industrial policy success: a large enough market, a capable government and enough public money; the authors say Indonesia has the first but needs help with the other two.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Provides a checklist for judging which emerging-market industrial policies are likely to succeed.
insights.quote: a large enough market, a capable government and enough public money
insights.locator: The World Bank’s chief economist, Indermit Gill

insights.claim: The authors urge Indonesia to ask the World Bank at the 12-18 October 2026 Bangkok annual meetings for cheaper long-term loans and guarantees for clean power and new factories, plus support for agencies that design, monitor and end industrial policies, with success judged by jobs, skills and wages rather than tonnes of nickel processed or investment announced.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: Signals potential demand for concessional and guarantee-backed financing of Indonesian clean power and processing.
insights.quote: ask both institutions to judge success by jobs, skills and wages, not by tonnes of nickel processed or investment dollars announced
insights.locator: On capacity, it should ask for help

insights.claim: Other Southeast Asian countries share Indonesia's fiscal limits and need for jobs, so they could jointly press the IMF and World Bank at the Bangkok meetings, the first in Southeast Asia since Bali in 2018, to support development-oriented green industrial plans.
insights.speaker: Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara
insights.so_what: A coordinated regional push could shift multilateral lending toward resource-based industrial strategies in ASEAN.
insights.quote: Other Southeast Asian countries face the same limits on money and the same need for jobs, so they can make this case together in Bangkok.
